35 of the 50 open-source AI agent repos I scan hit ASI03 — identity and privilege abuse. Not a rare edge case. A default outcome of how agent frameworks wire up credentials.

The OWASP GenAI Security Project's Agentic Security Initiative published the Top 10 for Agentic Applications in December 2025, built from over a year of work by 100+ contributors. It's a separate document from the OWASP LLM Top 10, and the distinction matters: the LLM list covers model risk, this one covers what happens once the model can act. Running LLM01 through LLM10 against your codebase does not mean you've covered agentic risk.

I wrote up each ASI category with what it actually looks like in code, plus where static analysis can catch it and where it genuinely can't. If you're building or reviewing agent codebases, worth the ten minutes.

https://asiscan.dev/blog/owasp-top-10-agentic-applications

#AIsecurity #AgenticAI #StaticAnalysis

Twenty-five of the fifty open-source AI agent repositories in our scan corpus had an ASI05 finding: unexpected code execution. Half.

Not half doing something exotic. Half doing the same three or four things, over and over: taking model output and passing it straight into exec(), eval(), or a shell command. Input validation doesn't catch it because the input isn't the problem — the model's output is, and by the time it reaches the exec() call it looks like ordinary program data.

We wrote up a real example: the exact shell command construction, why a reviewer would scan past it, and the fix that closes it without breaking the agent's ability to actually do things. ASIScan's rules for this pattern are also in the post, including what they flag and why.

If you're building or reviewing agent code that touches subprocess, exec, or shell commands, this one's worth ten minutes.

https://asiscan.dev/blog/asi05-unexpected-code-execution

#AIsecurity #AgentSecurity #StaticAnalysis
